interactions.summary: Jiang rejects timid student guesses and spells out the compulsive logic of possessive love: endless gifts, inducements, and pursuit followed by condemnation if refusal persists.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang-led exchange with brief student attempts.

speaker_notes.note: The ASR on this student line is garbled, but it functions as another failed guess that Jiang rejects before giving his own answer.

claims.claim: Jiang says possessive Virgilian love does not walk away from refusal; it escalates through gifts, luxury, spectacle, and persistence in order to force a yes.
The logic of this bad love is that rejection intensifies pursuit rather than correcting desire, because the lover treats refusal as a problem to overpower.
Jiang explicitly links this pattern back to Virgil's poetry by saying the rejected lover will eventually write the beloved into hell.
By asking how Dante differs immediately after this, Jiang frames Dantean love as the negation of coercive pursuit rather than just a milder version of it.

signature_moments.moment: Possessive love keeps upgrading the offer, from flowers to diamonds to the moon, because it cannot hear no.
signature_moments.source_phrase: flowers ... chocolates ... a diamond ring ... a Mercedes ... take her to the moon
signature_moments.why_it_matters: Jiang turns a moral distinction into a vivid comic sequence that exposes coercion hiding inside romance.

signature_moments.moment: The lover who cannot possess will eventually punish by narrative damnation.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It fuses erotic frustration, revenge, and literary production into one of the lecture's sharpest interpretive claims.

chronology_notes.note: This packet preserves one of the lecture's most memorable June 26 formulations of bad love: coercive escalation followed by retaliatory mythmaking or condemnation.

uncertainty_notes.note: The student's reference to a poem and a woman who refused to talk is too elliptical to ground a stronger literary identification, so it is left as part of the exploratory exchange rather than a standalone claim.
